text: Given an unsorted integer array, nums, return the smallest positive integer that is not present. You must run in linear time and use constant auxiliary space.

Thanks. Before I dive in, I'd like to clarify a few things. Just to confirm — positive means at least one, so zero and negatives never count as the answer, right? And the array can contain anything — negatives, zeros, duplicates, huge values?
Correct on both. Values span the full int range.

Here's the key observation I want to lock in first. With n elements, the answer is always between one and n plus one. If the array holds exactly one through n, the answer is n plus one; otherwise one of one through n is missing, and that's the answer. So any value at or below zero, or above n, is irrelevant — it can never be the answer.

Let me run the example: three, four, negative one, one. The present positives are one, three and four, so two is missing — answer two. And seven, eight, nine, eleven, twelve has no one, so the answer is one. Matches.

Let me think about the constraints for a second. The naive route is a hash set of all values, then probe one, two, and so on until one is missing — linear time, but linear space, which breaks the space rule. Sorting is n log n, which breaks the time rule. This problem reminds me of cyclic sort. Since the answer lives between one and n plus one, the array indices themselves can act as the hash table: put value v at index v minus one, and the first index whose value doesn't match is the gap.

Here's the plan. One: walk the array, carrying each value x in hand. Two: while x is between one and n, and its home, index x minus one, doesn't already hold x, swap x into its home and pick up whatever was there. Three: scan for the first index i where nums of i isn't i plus one, and return i plus one; if there is none, return n plus one. One thing worth flagging — the guard, x not equal to nums of x minus one, is load-bearing. Without it, a duplicate like one, one swaps one with an already-correct one forever — an infinite loop. And the nested while looks quadratic, but each swap fixes one value into its final home for good, so there are at most n swaps — amortized linear. Does this approach sound good, or would you rather I think of another way?

Alright, let me code this up. I'll use a copied value x as the hand that places elements home. The outer loop picks up each element; the while loop swaps x into its home and carries the old value onward, until x is out of range or already home. Then one scan finds the first mismatch. One detail worth flagging — the range check, x between one and n, must come before touching nums of x minus one; otherwise a negative or oversized x indexes out of bounds. The short-circuit and makes that order safe.

Let's dry-run the code on three, four, negative one, one, with n equal to four. Expected output two. The row that matters is the scan: after placing, the array is one, four, three, four. Index zero holds one, fine, but index one should hold two and holds a leftover four, so two is the smallest missing positive. That matches. Corner cases: a single one returns two. One, one returns two, and the guard prevents the infinite loop. Seven, eight, nine, eleven, twelve returns one, since nothing is in range and nothing moves. One, two, three returns four, falling through to n plus one.

Let me think about complexity here. Time is linear — amortized, since every swap finalizes one home that's never swapped out again, so there are at most n swaps, plus two linear scans. Space is constant — I mutate the input in place with just one scratch variable. Oh, one more thing — if mutating the input isn't allowed, I'd need a linear-space copy; the in-place trick is exactly what buys the constant space. And the same index-as-hash idea extends to finding all missing or duplicated numbers, sometimes with sign-marking instead of swaps.

Nicely done. Three things stood out: you pinned the one to n plus one bound before writing anything, you caught the duplicate infinite loop and why the guard fixes it, and you defended the amortized linear time against the looks-quadratic trap. Good work.
